title: Emphasis, cleft sentences and inversion
titleVi: Nhấn mạnh, câu chẻ và đảo ngữ
summary: Câu chẻ, đảo ngữ và trợ động từ nhấn mạnh — ba công cụ tạo trọng tâm câu ở band 8.
whyItMatters: Ở band 7, câu của bạn đúng nhưng phẳng: mọi ý nằm ngang hàng. Band 8 cần **trọng tâm**: *It is funding, not legislation, that determines outcomes*, *Never has the gap been wider*. Câu chẻ và đảo ngữ cho bạn cấu trúc C1 thật sự, nhưng chỉ khi dùng đúng — đảo ngữ sai trật tự gây lỗi nặng hơn một câu đơn giản.

sections.heading: It-clefts: putting one element in the spotlight
body: An **it-cleft** splits a sentence into a focus and a background: *The council approved the plan in 2019* → *It was **the council** that approved the plan in 2019* (focus on who) or *It was **in 2019** that the council approved the plan* (focus on when).
The frame is **It is/was + focus + that/who + rest**. Use **who** for people, **that** for everything else, including time and place: *It was in 2019 **that** the policy changed*, not *when*.

The pattern is especially useful for correction and contrast: *It is not the cost of treatment but the shortage of staff that limits access.* This single structure carries an argument that would otherwise need two sentences.

examples.right: It is the lack of affordable childcare that keeps women out of the labour market.
examples.wrong: It is the lack of affordable childcare who keeps women out of the labour market.

examples.right: It was in 2015 that the city introduced congestion charging.
examples.wrong: It was in 2015 when the city introduced congestion charging.
examples.note: The cleft uses **that**, even for time expressions.

examples.right: It is not the technology itself but the cost of maintenance that decides whether a project survives.

sections.heading: Wh-clefts: What ... is / What ... does
body: A **wh-cleft** begins with **What** and puts the new information at the end: *What the city needs is a reliable bus network.* The reader waits for the answer, which gives it weight.

Two patterns dominate. **What + subject + verb + be + noun**: *What shocked residents was the speed of the decision.* **What + subject + verb + be + verb**: *What the policy does is shift costs onto households.*
Use wh-clefts to define a problem before proposing a solution — the structure itself signals analysis: *What matters is not how much is spent but how evenly it is distributed.*

examples.right: What the report fails to explain is why the gap widened after 2010.
What the policy does is shift costs from employers to taxpayers.
examples.note: **What … does is + verb** — no *to* before the verb.

examples.right: What matters most is whether the scheme can be sustained.
examples.wrong: What matters most it is whether the scheme can be sustained.
examples.note: One focus marker only; do not add *it*.

sections.heading: Negative inversion: never, rarely, little, nowhere
body: When a **negative or restrictive adverbial** starts the sentence, the subject and auxiliary **invert**: *Never **have** I seen such rapid change.* *Rarely **does** the government admit error.* *Little **did** they realise how costly the scheme would be.*
If there is no auxiliary, add **do/does/did**: *Seldom **do** voters read the full manifesto.* The main verb stays in its base form after *do*.
These openers are rhetorical and should be rare in an essay — one per piece at most. Overuse reads as journalism, not academic analysis.

rows: Never has the city faced such pressure.
Little did voters know about the costs.
Nowhere is the gap more visible than in housing.
Not only + aux + subject + verb + but also
Not only did costs rise, but quality also fell.
No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than
No sooner had the scheme launched than demand surged.
Hardly had the report appeared when criticism followed.

sections.heading: Inversion after only, so, such and in conditionals
body: **Only + adverbial** at the front inverts the **main** clause: *Only when the data were rechecked **did** the error emerge.* *Only after the protest **did** the council publish the figures.*
**So + adjective** and **such + noun** can front a result clause with inversion: *So severe was the shortage that hospitals rationed beds.* *Such was the demand that the website crashed.*

Conditional inversion drops **if** and fronts the auxiliary: *Had I known about the deadline, I would have applied.* *Should you require further information, please contact the office.* *Were the policy reversed, thousands would lose cover.* This is formal and compact — ideal for conclusions.

examples.right: Only after the audit did the scale of the loss become clear.
examples.wrong: Only after the audit the scale of the loss became clear.
examples.note: **Only + adverbial** forces inversion in the main clause.

examples.right: So rapid was the decline that no policy could offset it.
Had the city invested earlier, the flooding would have been less severe.

sections.heading: even and do: quiet emphasis
body: **Even** signals that something is surprising relative to a scale: *Even wealthy households struggle with childcare costs.* Position matters — put it immediately before the element it emphasises: *Even **the minister** was unaware* versus *The minister was even **unaware*** (the latter is odd).

**Even though** concedes a fact; **even if** concedes a possibility: *Even though the scheme was funded, it failed* (it was funded) versus *Even if the scheme were funded, it would fail* (hypothetical).

**Do/does/did** adds emphatic force to a positive verb: *The evidence **does** suggest a link.* *The government **did** respond, though slowly.* Use it to rebut an implied doubt — sparingly, or it sounds defensive.

examples.right: Even the most experienced teachers found the new syllabus demanding.
Even though funding increased, waiting times did not fall.
examples.wrong: Even although funding increased, waiting times did not fall.

examples.right: The data do suggest that early intervention works.
examples.note: Emphatic **do** — rebuts the suspicion that the evidence is weak.

commonMistakes.wrong: It was in 2019 when the government changed the policy.
commonMistakes.right: It was in 2019 that the government changed the policy.
commonMistakes.why: Câu chẻ dùng **that** cho mọi thành phần, kể cả thời gian và nơi chốn. *When* chỉ dùng trong mệnh đề quan hệ, không dùng trong câu chẻ.

commonMistakes.wrong: Never I have seen such a rapid increase.
commonMistakes.right: Never have I seen such a rapid increase.
commonMistakes.why: Trạng từ phủ định đầu câu buộc **đảo ngữ**: trợ động từ trước chủ ngữ.

commonMistakes.wrong: Not only the cost rose, but the quality also fell.
commonMistakes.right: Not only did the cost rise, but the quality also fell.
commonMistakes.why: **Not only** đầu câu cũng gây đảo ngữ, và động từ chính trở về dạng nguyên mẫu sau *did*.

commonMistakes.wrong: Hardly I had arrived when the meeting began.
commonMistakes.right: Hardly had I arrived when the meeting began.
commonMistakes.why: Cấu trúc cố định **Hardly + had + subject + V3 + when**. Đảo ngữ là bắt buộc.

commonMistakes.wrong: What the city needs it is a reliable bus network.
commonMistakes.right: What the city needs is a reliable bus network.
commonMistakes.why: Câu chẻ *What …* đã có động từ *is* làm trung tâm; thêm *it* là lặp chủ ngữ.

ieltsTips: Dùng **it-cleft** để mở đoạn thân bài khi bạn muốn phản biện một quan điểm phổ biến: *It is not a lack of awareness but a lack of affordable options that sustains unhealthy diets.* Câu này tạo lập trường rõ ràng ngay từ câu đầu.
Dùng **wh-cleft** để định nghĩa vấn đề trước khi đề xuất giải pháp: *What developing cities lack is not ambition but fiscal space.* Giám khảo đọc thấy bạn biết tách nguyên nhân khỏi triệu chứng.
Dùng **conditional inversion** trong kết luận để câu văn trang trọng và gọn: ***Were** governments to invest in early education, the returns would outweigh the costs within a decade.*
Chỉ dùng **một** cấu trúc đảo ngữ trong cả bài. Nếu dùng *Never…*, *Not only…*, *Hardly…* liên tiếp, bài viết giống diễn văn hơn là phân tích học thuật.

exercises.question: ___ the shortage of staff that limits access to care.
exercises.explanation: It-cleft with a present claim: **It is … that**.

exercises.question: It was in 2015 ___ the city introduced congestion charging.
exercises.explanation: The cleft uses **that** even for time expressions.

exercises.question: Never ___ such a rapid decline in birth rates.
exercises.explanation: Negative fronting → inversion: **has the country seen**.

exercises.question: ___ the scheme were funded, it would still fail.
What the report fails to explain ___ why the gap widened.
exercises.explanation: **What … is** — singular agreement with the wh-clause.

exercises.question: Only after the audit ___ the scale of the loss become clear.
So severe ___ the shortage that hospitals rationed beds.
exercises.explanation: **So severe was the shortage that** — inverted result clause.

exercises.question: ___ I known about the deadline, I would have applied.
exercises.explanation: **Had I known** = If I had known.

exercises.question: The evidence ___ suggest that early intervention works.
